questions.question: A Grade 4 class in Chilliwack counts the salmon fry left in the classroom tank each day. Day 1: 60 fry, Day 2: 54 fry, Day 3: 48 fry, Day 4: 42 fry. If the pattern keeps going, how many fry will be in the tank on Day 5?
questions.explain: Find the change between two rows in the table (60 − 54 = 6), then subtract that same 6 from the last number: 42 − 6 = 36. A common trap is subtracting a different amount (like 4) or jumping two days ahead — always check your rule against every row of the table.

questions.question: Which number makes this equation true?  ___ + 8 = 23
questions.explain: To find a missing start number in an addition equation, undo the addition by subtracting: 23 − 8 = 15. The most common mistake is adding the two numbers you can see (23 + 8 = 31) — always check by putting your answer back in: 15 + 8 = 23.

questions.question: Ivy builds a row of triangles with craft sticks. Figure 1 uses 4 sticks, Figure 2 uses 7 sticks, and Figure 3 uses 10 sticks. Which rule describes this pattern?
options: Start at 4 and add 4 each time
Start at 3 and add 3 each time
Start at 4 and multiply by 2 each time
Start at 4 and add 3 each time
questions.explain: A pattern rule needs both the starting number and the change: the first figure has 4 sticks and each new figure adds 3 more (4, 7, 10). A common trap is using the change (3) as the starting number — test your rule by generating the numbers and comparing them to the picture.

questions.question: A lake near Kamloops is stocked with trout each week. The chart shows Week 1: 250 fish, Week 2: 400 fish, Week 3: 550 fish, Week 4: 700 fish. If the pattern continues, how many fish will be in the lake in Week 6?
questions.explain: The pattern increases by 150 each week, and Week 4 to Week 6 is two jumps: 700 + 150 + 150 = 1000. The most common mistake is counting the wrong number of jumps — stopping at Week 5 (850) or taking one jump too many (1150), so count the jumps, not the weeks.

questions.question: Maya wants a youth bus pass that costs $24. She has saved $17 so far. She writes the equation 17 + □ = 24. How much more money does Maya need?
questions.explain: To find the missing change amount, subtract what she has from the total: 24 − 17 = 7, and checking gives 17 + 7 = 24. The biggest trap is seeing a plus sign and adding the two numbers (17 + 24 = 41) — the plus sign tells you the story, but you still undo it to find the unknown.

questions.question: A Cub Scout pack is planning a 2-day hike near Sooke. Each of the 6 hikers needs 3 granola bars per day. How many granola bars does the pack need to bring in total?
questions.explain: Work out one day first (6 hikers × 3 bars = 18 bars), then multiply by the 2 days: 18 × 2 = 36 bars. The most common mistake is packing for only one day (18) — when planning per person, always ask 'how many people?' AND 'how many days?'

questions.question: Aiden has $45 in his piggy bank and adds $8 every week from his allowance. His sister Priya has $85 but spends $12 every week on snacks. If they both keep this up, after how many weeks will Aiden and Priya have the same amount of money?
questions.explain: Make a table with both patterns side by side: Aiden goes 45, 53, 61 while Priya goes 85, 73, 61 — they match at $61 after 2 weeks. The common trap is going one week too far (after 3 weeks Aiden has $69 but Priya only $49, so he has already passed her) — stop at the week where the two amounts are equal, not after.

questions.question: Ravi picked a basket of blackberries on the trail. He gave 14 berries to his neighbour, and then his brother added 9 more berries to the basket. Ravi now has 31 berries. How many berries did Ravi pick to start with?
questions.explain: Work backwards from 31 and undo each step in reverse order: undo the +9 (31 − 9 = 22), then undo the −14 (22 + 14 = 36). The most common mistake is repeating the story's operations forward on 31 (31 − 14 + 9 = 26) instead of undoing them — check your answer forwards: 36 − 14 = 22, and 22 + 9 = 31.
